resident.chief_complaint: Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months in a 41-year-old female with no history of trauma.
resident.history: A 41-year-old female with no history of trauma presented with weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months. Initial cervical noncontrast MRI showed a hyperintense intramedullary cord signal, with differential diagnoses including cervical spondylotic myelopathy and tumor. She was referred for an open biopsy of the cervical spinal cord to document the pathology of the tumor. At the time of transfer, she had severe spastic quadriparesis, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Follow-up MRI revealed cervical spondylosis with C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression associated with an extensive intramedullary high cord signal and cord enlargement on T2-weighted sagittal images extending from C5 to C7; axial images confirmed the intramedullary signal abnormality. T1-weighted MRI sagittal scan showed the lesion enhanced with contrast at the C5–C6 level.
resident.physical_exam: On examination at the time of transfer, severe spastic quadriparesis was present, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction were reported in the history. Detailed motor power, reflexes, sensation, and sphincter examination findings are not documented in the record.

imaging.public_message: I have not seen the films and am reporting only the case record's imaging description: cervical spondylosis with cord compression at C5-6 and C6-7, with extensive intramedullary T2 high signal and cord enlargement from C5 to C7. The record does not state compression direction or stenosis grade. These reported findings correlate highly with the described progressive myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord lesion at C5–C7, likely intramedullary, producing upper motor neuron signs in all four limbs. The upper extremity predominance suggests central cord involvement. Detailed motor, reflex, sensory, and sphincter examination findings are not documented, limiting precise localization.

red_flags.finding: Intramedullary cord enlargement and contrast enhancement at C5–C6 on MRI
red_flags.rationale: This suggests an intrinsic cord lesion (e.g., tumor, demyelination, inflammation) that could independently cause the progressive myelopathy; surgical decompression for spondylotic compression may not address the primary pathology, and biopsy or medical management may be needed.

In compressive cervical myelopathy from C5–C7 spondylosis, lower extremities are typically more affected due to longer corticospinal tracts; upper extremity predominance suggests a central cord or intramedullary process, reinforcing the likelihood of a primary cord lesion rather than compression alone.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The imaging shows C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression, but the clinical pattern of upper extremity-predominant spastic quadriparesis is atypical for compressive cervical myelopathy at those levels, which would be expected to affect lower limbs more; additionally, cord enlargement and contrast enhancement are not typical for simple spondylotic compression, suggesting an intramedullary lesion that better explains the symptoms.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: I remain the strongest advocate for conservative care. Given the progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, surgery is being considered, but before proceeding to irreversible intervention, I propose a formal, time-limited 3-6 month trial of intensive conservative management under close neurological monitoring. This would include supervised physical therapy for gait/balance/strength, occupational therapy for activities of daily living, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, and avoidance of high-risk activities. The literature on nonoperative management of cervical spondylotic myelopathy reports that a subset of patients—particularly those with mild symptoms and no rapid progression—can stabilize or improve without surgery; however, I acknowledge that severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter involvement and cord enhancement indicates a poorer prognosis for conservative care. Therefore, I define failure as any of the following: (1) no improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of strict conservative therapy; (2) new or worsening neurological deficits during the trial; (3) progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or enhancement on follow-up MRI at 3 months; or (4) inability to participate in therapy due to pain or functional decline. If any of these occur, I will accept that conservative management has failed and support surgical intervention or biopsy as appropriate. Until then, I hold my stance for a trial of conservative care.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Deputy Director has cited progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction as grounds for urgent surgery, asserting that a conservative trial is not safe. I have already weighed these findings: they indicate a poorer prognosis and demand close monitoring, which is exactly why my proposed conservative trial includes strict neurological oversight and predefined failure criteria—including no improvement or further deterioration after 3 months, new deficits, or imaging progression. They do not, however, constitute an absolute contraindication to a time-limited conservative attempt; some patients with myelopathy, even with sphincter involvement, can stabilize. No new finding from the record has been presented that changes this balance. I therefore hold my stance for a formal 3-6 month conservative trial with early surgical conversion if failure criteria are met.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is progressive severe cervical myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction and an enhancing intramedullary lesion at C5-C6. The clinical course and enhancement pattern indicate that a 3-6 month conservative trial carries an unacceptable risk of irreversible neurological worsening, and surgical decompression with tissue diagnosis is needed without delay. The upper extremity predominance does suggest intrinsic cord pathology, so biopsy during surgery is essential.
proposed_options: Urgent C5-C7 anterior decompression and fusion with intraoperative biopsy of the enhancing C5-C6 lesion.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent C5-C7 anterior decompression and fusion with intraoperative biopsy of the enhancing C5-C6 lesion.

director_rulings.surgical_plan: Urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion at C5-C7 (ACDF C5-C6 and C6-C7 or C6 corpectomy as determined intraoperatively) with biopsy of the enhancing intramedullary lesion at C5-C6. If biopsy reveals neoplasm or inflammatory disease, appropriate specialist referral will follow after stabilization.
